title: reset: soft, mixed, hard
summary: git reset moves the branch pointer, and optionally the index and working tree with it. Three modes, three levels of danger.

steps.title: reset moves the branch
body: `git reset <commit>` moves **the current branch** (and so HEAD) to another commit. The mode says how much else follows:
```text
before:  A---B---C   main, HEAD          git reset --soft HEAD~1
after:   A---B   main, HEAD                   (C is no longer on any branch)
C
| Mode | Branch moves | Index reset | Working tree reset |
| `--soft` | yes | no | no |
| `--mixed` (default) | yes | yes | no |
| `--hard` | yes | yes | **yes** |
So after undoing commit C:
- `--soft`: C's changes are still **staged**. Ready to recommit.
- `--mixed`: C's changes are in your files but **unstaged**.
- `--hard`: C's changes are **gone** from index and disk (the commit is still in the reflog).

steps.prompt: You just made three small commits that should have been one. Which command lets you recommit them as a single commit, with all their changes already staged?
steps.explain: `--soft` moves the branch back three commits but leaves the index as it was, so the combined changes of all three are staged. `--hard` would throw the changes away.

steps.prompt: History: `A---B---C (main)`, a clean working tree, and C added the line `log()` to `app.cs`. You run `git reset HEAD~1` (no mode). What does `git status -s` print, and where does `main` point? Answer with two lines: the status line, then `main -> X`.
steps.explain: The default is `--mixed`: the branch and the index go back to B, the working tree keeps C's version. So `app.cs` differs from the index but nothing is staged.

steps.prompt: Same start (`A---B---C`, clean). This time: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`. What does `git status -s` print?
steps.explain: Only the branch moves. The index still holds C's snapshot, so C's change is staged relative to the new HEAD (B).

steps.prompt: After `git reset <mode> HEAD~1` on a clean tree, where are the last commit's changes?
steps.explain: Read the table top to bottom: each mode resets one more area.

steps.title: Using reset safely
body: Three everyday uses:
```bash
git reset                     # unstage everything (mixed reset to HEAD itself)
git reset --soft HEAD~1       # undo the last commit, keep it staged
git reset --hard origin/main  # make my branch exactly match the remote, throwing away local work
Rules that keep you out of trouble:
1. `--hard` is the only mode that destroys work, and only **uncommitted** work is truly unrecoverable. Run `git status` first.

2. `reset` **rewrites history** on your branch: the commits after the target are no longer on it. Fine for commits that exist only on your machine. For commits you already **pushed**, teammates may have built on them; use `git revert` instead (next lesson).

steps.prompt: Match each situation to the right reset.
pairs: I staged the wrong files and want to start staging again
Undo my last local commit but keep its changes staged
Undo my last local commit and edit the files before staging again
My local branch is a mess; make it match the server exactly

steps.prompt: You run `git reset --hard HEAD~1` with uncommitted edits in two files. Which is true?
options: The last commit can be recovered from the reflog, but the two files' uncommitted edits are lost
Everything can be recovered from the reflog
Git refuses to reset with uncommitted changes
steps.explain: Commits live in the object database and the reflog remembers where branches pointed. Uncommitted edits were never saved as objects, so `--hard` overwrote them. Commit or stash first.

steps.prompt: Complete the commands: unstage everything, then undo the last two commits but keep all their changes staged.
steps.explain: `HEAD~2` is two commits back. `HEAD^2` would mean the second parent of a merge, a different thing.

steps.title: Three resets, for real
prompt: Two repos, and each needs a different reset.
**`~/api`**: the last three commits (`WIP`, `WIP 2`, `more WIP`) should be **one** commit called `Add request logging`, directly on top of `Add rate limiter`, holding all of their work.
Careful: `secrets.env` is staged by mistake. It must **not** end up in any commit, but keep the file on disk.
**`~/spike`**: the experiment failed. Make `main` exactly `Stable version` again, with no leftover edits.
Start each with `git status` and `git log --oneline`.

checks.name: ~/api ends in one "Add request logging" commit on top of "Add rate limiter"
checks.cmd: cd ~/api && test "$(git log -1 --format=%s)" = "Add request logging" && test "$(git log -1 --format=%s HEAD~1)" = "Add rate limiter"
checks.fail: The top of `~/api` is not yet one `Add request logging` commit right after `Add rate limiter`. `git log --oneline` shows what you have.

checks.name: it holds all the WIP work
checks.fail: Some of the WIP work is missing from the new commit. A soft reset keeps every change staged, ready to commit again.

checks.name: secrets.env stayed out of Git, and on disk
checks.cmd: cd ~/api && test -f secrets.env && test -z "$(git log --all --format=%H -- secrets.env)" && ! git diff --cached --name-only | grep -qx secrets.env
checks.fail: `secrets.env` was committed or is still staged (or the file is gone). Unstage it before you commit; if it got committed, reset again.

checks.name: ~/spike is back at "Stable version"
checks.fail: `main` in `~/spike` is not at `Stable version` yet.

checks.name: ~/spike has no leftover edits
checks.fail: `git status` in `~/spike` still shows changes. Which reset mode also resets the working tree?

hints: In `~/api`, deal with the secret first: `git restore --staged secrets.env` (or the mixed reset `git reset secrets.env`) unstages it.
`git reset --soft HEAD~3` moves the branch back three commits and keeps all their changes staged; one `git commit -m` then makes the single commit.
In `~/spike`, `git reset --hard HEAD~2` moves the branch and throws away both the commits and the uncommitted edits.
steps.explain: Soft keeps everything staged (squash), mixed unstages (the default, also per file), hard throws away the working tree too. Before any `--hard`, run `git status`: committed work can come back from the reflog, uncommitted work cannot.
